issues.legal_issue: The agreement created a lease rather than a licence, making the civil eviction suit by the owner not maintainable against the protected tenant.
material_facts: The occupier was put in possession under a written agreement described as a leave-and-licence agreement, and its parties were described as licensor and licensee.
The agreement required regular monthly payments, prohibited subletting or parting with possession without consent, and provided for renewal at the occupier’s will.
The occupier had exclusive possession; the owner’s notice to vacate followed several years after the agreement expired.
There was no relationship or friendship between the parties that explained the occupier’s presence apart from the payments made for use and occupation.
The owner brought a civil suit for eviction on the basis that the occupier was a licensee; the occupier claimed protection as a tenant under rent-control legislation.
The trial court and first appellate court treated the agreement as a licence, and the High Court dismissed the second appeal.
issues.conclusion: The agreement was in reality a lease, and the occupier was a month-to-month tenant protected by the rent-control legislation; accordingly, the civil suit was not maintainable and the eviction decree was set aside.
issues.legal_principle: The substance of an instrument, not its label, determines whether it creates a lease or a licence. The central test is the parties’ intention: creation of an interest in the property indicates a lease, whereas permission to use the property while legal possession remains with the owner indicates a licence. Exclusive possession is relevant and gives rise to a prima facie inference of tenancy, but is not conclusive. Rent-control legislation should be interpreted to advance tenant protection and prevent landlords from defeating that protection through the form or drafting of an agreement. The Court applied Associated Hotels of India Ltd. v. R.N. Kapoor, [1960] 1 SCR 368, and Sohan Lal Naraindas v. Laxmidas Raghunath Gadit, [1971] 3 SCR 319; it explained Shell-Mex and BP Ltd. v. Manchester Garages Ltd., [1971] 1 All E.R. 841. Under section 56 of the Goa, Daman and Diu Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1968, the civil suit was not maintainable in the circumstances found.

rule.if: civil_eviction_suit and rent_control_protection_applies and exclusive_possession and monthly_rent_paid and subletting_restricted and renewal_at_occupier_will and rent_was_transactional_consideration

predicates.civil_eviction_suit: The property owner brought a civil suit seeking eviction of the occupier.
predicates.rent_control_protection_applies: The occupier claimed, and the Court found, protection as a tenant under applicable rent-control legislation.
predicates.exclusive_possession: The occupier had exclusive possession of the premises.
predicates.monthly_rent_paid: The agreement required the occupier to make regular monthly payments for occupation.
predicates.subletting_restricted: The agreement restricted the occupier from subletting or parting with possession without the owner’s consent.
predicates.renewal_at_occupier_will: The agreement provided for renewal at the occupier’s will.
predicates.rent_was_transactional_consideration: The payments for use and occupation were the sole consideration for the arrangement.

issues.definition: When a civil eviction suit concerns an occupier protected as a tenant and the stated possession and agreement facts establish a tenancy, the suit is not maintainable.

issues.legal_issue: Whether the classification of an agreement as a licence rather than a lease is a factual finding binding in a second appeal when the nature of possession depends on interpreting the agreement.
material_facts: The trial court and first appellate court classified the written agreement as a licence.
The High Court dismissed the second appeal on the ground that the lower courts’ concurrent findings were findings of fact.
The nature of the occupier’s possession depended on the correct interpretation of the written agreement.
issues.conclusion: The lower courts’ findings were not findings of fact binding on the High Court in second appeal; the nature of possession depended on correct interpretation of the agreement.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 100 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, concurrent findings of fact ordinarily bind the High Court in second appeal, but the classification at issue was not such a finding because the nature of possession depended on interpretation of the document. The document therefore had to be correctly construed to determine whether it created a lease or a licence.

predicates.second_appeal: The matter came before the High Court in a second appeal.
predicates.concurrent_lower_court_classification: The trial court and first appellate court reached the same classification of the agreement.
predicates.document_interpretation_controls_nature_: The legal nature of the occupier’s possession depended on interpreting the written agreement.

issues.definition: When a second appeal challenges a concurrent classification that depends on interpreting an agreement to determine the nature of possession, that classification is not binding as a finding of fact.
